blocks.text: 沙箱的设计
虚拟机和容器⁠（在新窗口打开）是实现沙箱的两种常见机制，但 Codex 沙箱走的是另一条路。Codex 不把计算搬到独立环境来实现隔离，而是利用各平台自带的沙箱能力，约束在用户现有环境中运行的命令。

blocks.text: 对许多开发者来说，自己的笔记本电脑就是一套量身定制的开发环境，可以随时按需改动。要在 Docker 容器里复现这套环境并不轻松，而且有些工作流仍然依赖运行在宿主机上的工具。

inlines.text: 对许多开发者来说，自己的笔记本电脑就是一套量身定制的开发环境，可以随时按需改动。要在 Docker 容器里复现这套环境并不轻松，而且有些工作流仍然依赖运行在宿主机上的工具。

blocks.text: 举个例子：在 Mac 上用 Codex 开发 iOS 应用。如果你决定把 Codex 放进 Docker 里运行来实现沙箱隔离，Codex 就无法运行由 Mac 原生可执行文件组成的 iOS 构建工具链，也无法启动 iPhone 模拟器来运行代码。基于 Docker 的工作流可以把构建和模拟器操作交给 Mac 宿主机执行，但这些操作会在容器沙箱之外运行，需要另行施加限制。对 Codex 来说，我们更愿意把事情做简单：在操作系统层面的沙箱上重点投入，让 Codex 能在最适合当前任务的环境中运行。

blocks.text: Codex 沙箱实现
沙箱实现会把权限配置转化为由操作系统强制执行的各种限制。网络代理的核心请求处理与策略逻辑在三大主流操作系统上共用，而代理的搭建方式以及与沙箱的集成则因操作系统而异。我们先看共用的代理部分，再分别介绍 macOS、Linux 和 Windows 上的实现。

inlines.text: 沙箱实现会把权限配置转化为由操作系统强制执行的各种限制。网络代理的核心请求处理与策略逻辑在三大主流操作系统上共用，而代理的搭建方式以及与沙箱的集成则因操作系统而异。我们先看共用的代理部分，再分别介绍 macOS、Linux 和 Windows 上的实现。

blocks.text: 网络代理
为了落实权限配置中的网络限制，harness 会启动一个网络代理，并把沙箱配置成允许连接到该代理、同时阻止直接连接外部主机。代理会按配置中的域名规则逐一检查每个请求，决定是否转发。

inlines.text: 为了落实权限配置中的网络限制，harness 会启动一个网络代理，并把沙箱配置成允许连接到该代理、同时阻止直接连接外部主机。代理会按配置中的域名规则逐一检查每个请求，决定是否转发。

blocks.text: 在 Codex 仓库中，网络代理实现在 codex-network-proxy⁠(opens in a new window) crate 里，harness 以库的形式使用它，不过它也可以构建成 独立 CLI⁠(opens in a new window)。启用后，codex-network-proxy 默认会同时启动一个 HTTP 代理和一个 SOCKS5 代理。这些代理地址通过环境变量传给沙箱启动的进程。除了注入 HTTP_PROXY、HTTPS_PROXY、ALL_PROXY 等标准环境变量外，还会注入一批常见的应用专用环境变量⁠(opens in a new window)（例如 PIP_PROXY）。诚然，并非所有程序都会遵循这些环境变量。如果程序试图直接连接外部主机，操作系统的沙箱限制会将其拦截，具体机制见下文各平台章节。

At OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a new window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex⁠(opens in a new window), to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control.

blocks.text: Designing the s andbox

Virtual machines and containers⁠(opens in a new window) are two popular mechanisms used for sandboxing, but we take a different approach with the Codex sandbox. Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.

blocks.text: For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

inlines.text: For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

blocks.text: For example, consider using Codex to develop an iOS app on a Mac. If you decided to sandbox Codex by running it inside Docker, Codex would not be able to run the iOS build toolchain composed of native Mac executables, nor could it launch the iPhone simulator to run the code. A Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host, but those operations would execute outside the container’s sandbox and would need their own restrictions. For Codex, we prefer to keep things simple by investing heavily in OS-specific sandboxing so Codex can run in the environment that is most appropriate to the task at hand.

blocks.text: Codex sandbox implementation

The sandbox implementation turns a permission profile into restrictions enforced by the operating system. The network proxy’s core request-handling and policy logic is shared across all three major operating systems, while proxy setup and integration with the sandbox are OS-specific. We’ll examine the shared proxy first, followed by the implementations for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

blocks.text: Network proxy

To enforce a permission profile’s network restrictions, the harness starts a network proxy and configures the sandbox to allow connections to it while blocking direct connections to external hosts. The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

blocks.text: In the Codex repo, the network proxy is implemented in the codex-network-proxy⁠(opens in a new window) crate, which the harness uses as a library, though it can also be built as a standalone CLI⁠(opens in a new window). When enabled, codex-network-proxy starts both an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy by default. These proxy addresses are communicated to the process spawned by the sandbox via environment variables. In addition to injecting standard environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY, a number of well-known application-specific environment variables⁠(opens in a new window) (such as PIP_PROXY) are injected, as well. Admittedly, not all programs honor these environment variables. If a program attempts a direct connection to an external host, the operating system’s sandbox restrictions block it, as described in the platform-specific sections below.

MXC’s filesystem policy denies access by default. Codex therefore adds read-only grants for the local drive roots to provide the broad reads allowed by this profile. These grants apply recursively, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions.

blocks.text: Deny globs

MXC takes concrete deny paths only, so Codex expands deny globs to matching files and directories before launch. New paths that match the glob are not automatically added while the command is running.

blocks.text: Network access

Domain rules such as *.openai.com are enforced by the shared Codex network proxy described earlier. Codex runs that proxy outside the sandbox and passes its addresses to the command through the same standard *_PROXY environment variables as mentioned previously. MXC blocks direct external connections while allowing host-loopback connections, including access to the proxy. Other local services remain reachable.

blocks.text: Writing and executing code gives agents a flexible way to solve problems beyond software development. The Codex sandbox lets them use that capability in the user’s existing environment with explicit limits on filesystem and network access. It is a reusable primitive within the harness, and the codex sandbox command makes it available to tools you build yourself.

blocks.text: As agents take on more tasks, we want to make sandboxing practical for more tools and environments. Our goal is to expand what agents can do while keeping people in control of what they can access.
